subtype: Approach: contain by changing passwords and turning on two-factor login [Action]
passage:
Sit down, Ishita, and let me tell you about something I did right when I was twenty-two. I'm Shankar, and back then I got an email from an online shop saying their system had been breached. My first instinct was to put the phone down and hope.

Instead I opened the site, changed my password straight away, and then remembered I had used that same password for my email. So I changed it there too, and on two other accounts. Then I found the setting that asks for a second code when someone logs in and switched it on for all of them. It took forty minutes.

A month later a friend's account from the same shop was emptied. Mine wasn't touched.

qa.q: How long did it take Shankar to change the passwords and turn on the second code?
What was Shankar's first instinct on reading the breach email, and what made a difference?
qa.a: Shankar's first instinct was to freeze and hope, but remembering the reused password pushed Shankar to act at once.

qa.q: What turning point in the story showed a wise choice, and what alternative could have followed?
qa.a: The turning point was remembering the same password on the email account and changing it there too; otherwise the breach could have spread to more accounts.

qa.q: How did the friend's emptied account differ from Shankar's after the breach?
qa.a: The friend's account was emptied while Shankar's was untouched, which shows that quick action limited the damage.

grounding: After a company's breach email, the person changes the password everywhere it was reused and turns on two-factor login at once.

The email arrived at 11:40 p.m., the night before Aadhya's semester exam: the food-ordering app she used had been breached, and 'passwords may have been exposed'. The hostel internet was crawling.
Her first thought was to deal with it after the exam. Then she remembered: she used that same password for her email and her college portal. If someone had it, they might already be trying.
Gurleen, her roommate, held the phone torch while Aadhya worked through it on patchy mobile data. First, a new password on the food app. Then her email, the most important one, because every other reset goes through it. Then the college portal and a shopping site where she had reused it. Each new password different.
Last, she switched on two-step login for her email and the portal, so a code would come to her phone even if someone had a password.
It took forty minutes. At 12:25 she put the phone down. 'Now I can sleep,' she said, and did.

qa.q: When did the breach email arrive?
qa.a: At 11:40 p.m., the night before the exam.

qa.q: Why did Aadhya decide not to wait until after the exam?
qa.a: She felt uneasy realising the same password guarded her email and college portal, and worried someone might already be trying.

qa.q: Why did Aadhya change her email password right after the app's?
qa.a: Every other reset goes through email, so securing it protects the rest of her accounts.

qa.q: What is the night like for Gurleen?
qa.a: Gurleen stays up holding the torch, probably tired but glad to help Aadhya finish before sleeping.

grounding: Shows a young person changing the breached password and every reused one at once and turning on two-step login to limit damage.

Wasim was on the Metro to Nehru Place when the message came: the movie-ticket site he used had 'identified unauthorised access', and he should change his password.
He got off at the next station and sat on a bench. He knew the problem at once. That password, his cat's name and his birth year, was the same on his email, his bank's app and his work portal.
He called his sister Jyoti, who worked in IT. 'Do it in order,' she said. 'Ticket site first. Then email. Then everything else that used it.'
So he did, right there on the platform, trains rushing past. Ticket site: new password. Email: new password, different. Bank app: new. Work portal: new. For each, he turned on two-step login, so a code would come to his phone.
It took twenty-five minutes, and three trains went by. When he finally boarded one, his phone showed a code request from the ticket site. Someone had tried the old password. It didn't work.

qa.q: What was Wasim's old password made of?
qa.a: His cat's name and his birth year.

qa.q: How might Wasim have felt when the code request appeared?
qa.a: Alarmed that someone had tried, and relieved that the new password and two-step login stopped them.

qa.q: Why did Jyoti's 'do it in order' advice help?
qa.a: It had Wasim secure the breached site and then his email, which guards everything else, before the other reused accounts.

qa.q: How might Jyoti feel hearing later about the blocked attempt?
qa.a: Relieved and glad her quick advice made a real difference.

grounding: Shows a young person changing a breached password and every reused one immediately and enabling two-step login, blocking a later attempt.
